thread.title: Apple: The Ultimate Buy And Hold - Apple AAPL)

author: MangoTree Analysis
title: Apple: The Ultimate Buy And Hold - Apple AAPL)
text:
Disastrous Q1 Confirms iPhone Skepticism On January 2nd, the second day of 2019, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) released a bombshell onto the tech and financial world.
Actual Guidance My Estimates Revenue $84 bln $91 bln (midpoint) $89.42 bln Gross Margin (%) 38.0% 38.0-38.5% 38.3% OpEx $8.7 bln $8.75 bln (midpoint) $8.72 bln EPS $3.97 ~$4.50 $4.42 Obviously, the "actual" numbers are subject to change as the quarter progresses, but as you can see, Apple reported a quarter that missed both its guidance and my cautious expectations ... badly.
Frankly, the stock ought to have been punished. Delivering a disastrous report like the one Apple delivered especially after stacking quarter upon quarter of positive "beat-and-raise" results is a disappointment to say the least.
In my opinion though, management is blaming the wrong issues for the miss on revenue.
The Miss Was 100% iPhone Related Apple blamed four key factors for its massive revenue shortfall:
iPhone launch timing Currency headwinds Supply constraints Emerging market weakness According to the bombshell letter, the first two factors were already priced into its guidance, but the last two had a greater-than-projected impact. The last factor in particular led the shortfall.
The first two factors are reasonable, but seemed to have a minimal impact on Apple's miss. It was the last two factors that drove this weakness. Even then, however, I believe blaming supply constraints and a weaker China is somewhat of a straw man argument to shift blame away from the real problem with weak iPhone sales.
With regards to supply constraints, if Apple was having production issues, then why was there speculation earlier on in the year that there were layoffs taking place at the iPhone production facilities? If demand for new products was outpacing Apple's ability to supply these products, why would Apple's manufacturing partners be (allegedly) laying off workers?
In terms of emerging markets weakness (i.e., China), I believe Apple may be taking the easy road by blaming a weak Chinese smartphone market/overall economy for more severe demand challenges. Though I acknowledge that the ongoing economic slowdown and higher tariffs negatively impacted Apple's "Greater China" segment, I do not believe management should blame the brunt of this miss on China. I believe the miss came from weak all-around demand for iPhones.
In the sit down between Josh Lipton and Apple CEO Tim Cook, Mr. Cook mentions that Apple wished it performed better in its developed markets (i.e., North America, Europe, etc.) than it did.
There was a multitude of factors that contributed to the miss on iPhone weakness including macroeconomic weakness and trade tensions in China. But to blame a great deal of the weakness in my view is not the right approach. We'll know more when Apple releases its results by geography, but until then, we know that the warning signs on North American demand persisted throughout the quarter.
The Timeline of Events Leading Up To The Miss It all started really when at the end of fiscal Q4, during the conference call , Luca Maestri, Apple's CFO, disclosed that the company was going to end unit sales reporting. This sparked fears about potential weakness on the iPhone heading into the all-important holiday quarter.
Third, starting with the December quarter, we will no longer be providing unit sales data for iPhone, iPad and Mac.
This comment placed towards the middle of the conference call sparked fears about demand for Apple's various hardware products, particularly the iPhone.
Then, on November 5th, Nikkei released a report saying Apple was telling manufacturing partners to cancel a planned iPhone XR production boost. It reportedly told partners Foxconn and Pegatron to halt plans for additional production lines specific to the iPhone XR.
On November 9th, Skyworks (NASDAQ: SWKS ) delivered a disappointing Q4 guidance citing premium smartphone softness. On the same day, KeyBanc downgraded Apple supplier Synaptics (NASDAQ: SYNA ) off the back of weakening iPhone XR sell-throughs observed through KeyBanc's survey work.
Then, on November 12th, Apple's 3D sensing laser provider, Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE ), lowered its guidance substantially after a large customer reduced orders for these sensors.
On the same day, the sell-side begins reacting (via running checks). Longbow indicates order cuts of 20-30% for the iPhone XR and XS Max. Well-known Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo cut his iPhone XR estimate by 30% from 100 mln to 70 mln through to September of 2019.
The next day, Goldman (NYSE: GS ) cuts iPhone estimates, believing Lumentum's aforementioned guidance cut came mostly from the iPhone. Goldman proceeded to cut iPhone estimates by 6% for 2019.
On the 13th, yet another Apple supplier, Qorvo (NASDAQ: QRVO ), cut its revenue guidance by ~8% while cutting EPS outlook by ~13%. Management cited "recent demand changes or flagship smartphones."
On the 15th, Austrian based Apple supplier, AMS, cut its own guidance, citing "recent demand changes from a major consumer customer."
On the 19th, the Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was, again, cutting production for the iPhone XR.
A little over a week later, out comes yet another analyst cutting its iPhone unit targets. Canaccord cut its price target from $250 to $225 after its survey work suggested weak initial iPhone XR sales.
Then, on December 4th, Bloomberg puts out the "fire drill" report saying that it was moving around marketing executives to boost iPhone sales.
A couple days later, UBS says that according to its surveys, iPhone purchase intent is at a five-year low with particular weakness in the US and China.
After this point, multiple analysts (including Ming-Chi Kuo) cut targets, and some suppliers lower guidance.
The bottom line is there were warnings that iPhone demand would underwhelm expectations .
The Longer-Term Picture For The iPhone I am of the belief that the iPhone is in a bust cycle similar to that of the 2016 cycle, when in 2016's second quarter, iPhone shipments fell by a staggering 16%. The key word there is "cycle". iPhone sales from year to year are determined by Apple's ability to innovate and create quality iPhones for the price they are sold at. 59% of Apple's fiscal Q4 revenue was iPhone generated. Having a product that represents three-fifths of your revenue be cyclical is worrying, as recurrently higher revenues are hard to generate.
Meanwhile, the overall smartphone market is beginning to flatten out.
(Source: IDC )
In 2018, global smartphone shipments were slightly negative, while high-end smartphones suffered the most.
Despite that, IDC is projecting a reacceleration in shipment growth to ~3.5% this year, and then furthered to 4% next year as more and more phone makers move to 5G. The global smartphone market has been mostly neutral, and while that is not as a bad as negative, its double-digit growth days are behind it. The iPhone has a key headwind however that could factor into continued weakness in sales.
Apple is a victim of its own success. Because Apple makes such quality iPhones, the user is able to hold onto the phone for an increased period of time. Why is this a problem? Because there only three ways that Apple can pick up new unit sales:
First-time smartphone buyers From its competition Older users upgrading First-time smartphone buyers have a plethora of choices on the market, and do not factor into new iPhone sales as they would have in the early days of the smartphone market.
On the second point, picking up users from the competition (mostly Android) is an extremely difficult thing to do. Not only are you changing the user's hardware out, you are changing out their whole experience. While a traditional iOS user may use a certain suite of iOS application, an Android user switching to iOS may have an increasingly difficult time using the apps in the iOS ecosystem. That is the key word, ecosystem. The Android and iOS ecosystems are so solid that changing operating systems (and phones) will be a difficult transition for the user.
Lastly, Apple can increase sales as older users upgrade their smartphones.
The problem is Apple, by creating longer-lasting iPhone products, has allowed users to take their time with upgrades. Coupled with lofty price points on iPhones, and you get a lower interest in general for users to upgrade their iPhone. We are beginning to see users upgrade their phones once every three years instead of two years. This elongation of the upgrade cycle creates air pockets of demand that temporarily impact iPhone sales in a negative manner. Unless Apple finds an innovative piece of software that can completely disrupt the current iPhone, this upgrade cycle will continue to elongate.
Right now, the iPhones being upgraded are mostly from the iPhone 6S family, a particular iPhone model that was a flop, with iPhone units declining double digits during the time the 6S was sold.
(Source: Recode )
At the time, people were worried that the iPhone's best and most innovative days were behind it. As time went on, these skeptics were proven wrong, as Apple made incremental improvements to its iPhones.
The problem is upgrade volume for XR (the phone most 6S users would upgrade to) is weak because the 6S was such a weak seller. The biggest catalyst for unit growth was going to come in weak this year.
On top of that, the iPhone X cycle had a plethora of users looking to upgrade devices, as this cycle was two years after the hit iPhone 6. This made comparing iPhone units on a Y/Y basis tough for Apple, as the number of upgradable devices slid. Couple with the fact that ASPs were already high on iPhones last year (and only grew this year) and no new major technological innovations were present in the new iPhone lineup, and you get an iPhone cycle with much less demand.
We now have to look to 2019 to see where the iPhone will be. Looking back at past "S" model years (most recently the iPhone 6S), we get a flat to slightly positive unit sale count the year after. I'm expecting potential for continued weakness into the next iPhone cycle. According to Ming-Chi Kuo, we should expect three identically sized models as this year's. Unless we get some new software feature or hardware redesign, I doubt we get a positive year for iPhone shipments. Right now though, Apple is in the prototype phase of iPhone development if we should expect a new launch this fall.
However, if this is another "S" year, with minimal improvements in the technology and/or the design, we should expect lowered unit sales on a Y/Y growth basis. This would be the first time that Apple ever held back-to-back negative years for iPhone units.
As I already mentioned, the expectation is that Apple will continue to sell three models of the same screen sizes as the iPhone XR/XS/and XS Max. If this holds up, and there is no new major feature, Apple may need to cut prices on these phones to drive satisfactory unit sales.
Turning to the 2020 iPhone launch cycle, however, we see potential for rejuvenated unit growth from the iPhone. 2020 is the year Apple is expected to use 5G hardware in its new iteration of smartphones. While other phones from other smartphone developers are expected to incorporate 5G hardware this year in 2019, there may be one key reason for Apple delaying the launch of its 5G iPhone until next year.
The most obvious reason is that Apple normally waits for carriers to develop the infrastructure that would run this new telecommunications standard. Right now, carriers are deploying 5G in a minimal fashion to customers, as they continue to build out infrastructure into 2020-2021. So the key selling point of these major smartphone makers the fact that they are 5G compatible may not come to fruition if carriers haven't deployed this infrastructure.
While 5G remains smartphone makers' talking points into 2019, real deployment will not come until next year. This could mean strength from iPhone towards the back of 2020.
Another catalyst for further iPhone sales reversal is the launch of another iteration of the hit iPhone SE.
(Source: Macworld UK )
The launch of a second generation iPhone SE could further sales in the years to come. While I do not believe Apple will add a new iPhone SE to its lineup in 2019 (same models in '19 as the XR/XS/Max), the potential for Apple to launch an iPhone SE in 2020 could further add to an already strong iPhone cycle. You combine highly upgraded hardware and software features from 5G deployment in iPhones, with a new version of the hit iPhone SE, and you could have a phenomenal super cycle year for Apple.
A key reason that the iPhone SE was such a hit seller was its low starting price of just $399. In contrast, the lowest-priced phone Apple currently retails (iPhone 7) starts at $449 with minimal memory. If, in 2020, Apple re-introduces the iPhone SE on an updated iOS operating system (with Face ID and all the other cool features) and a compelling price, I believe that we could see a drastic turnaround in iPhone shipments.
As such, I believe the 2020 iPhone launch could be the catalyst that propels iPhone sales once again. After that, iPhone units are anyone's guess.
Does Apple's Culture of Innovation Still Exist? This is a question that has been asked about Apple for the last few years, as critics accuse Apple of pumping out less and less innovative products for higher and higher prices to keep investors happy.
Under Steve Jobs, the general belief was that Apple had a culture of innovation. Apple in many cases singlehandedly created or disrupted industries. It disrupted/created the PC, the smartphone, the tablet, the smartwatch, and it created the iPod.
Thus, Apple's stock has skyrocketed over the years, despite the recent plunge in share price:
AAPL data by YCharts
While Tim Cook has argued that Apple has more things to come from both hardware and software, Apple has not singlehandedly disrupted or created a new industry really since Tim Cook took over. Don't get me wrong, Tim Cook has done marvelous things for Apple's business. Phenomenal price appreciation and strong growth in the business have only been sustained by Apple's ability to consistently innovate. Of late, Apple's Mac and iPad sales have been deteriorating, with the iPhone soon to follow. Every single year, Apple is judged based on its ability to deliver a product that not only justifies its high price, but is also substantially better than the previous version of that product.
In my personal opinion, Apple's closest thing to innovation of late has been the AirPods, which have not necessarily shaken up industries like previous Apple products have. I believe Apple has things in the works, but most of these products are software related.
Apple's Future: Software Apple, since inception, has generated the vast majority of its overall revenue from hardware products. Hardware, especially technology-related hardware, is a cyclical business, depending on product refreshes and market share grabs to grow revenue. Software has disrupted this, creating a recurring revenue opportunity for Apple. The real question is how do you value Apple? Do you value Apple as a cyclical hardware technology company that depends on increasingly innovative product cycles to generate revenue? Or is Apple a software business that is deserving of a higher multiple.
In my opinion, Apple is turning into the ultimate show-me story. If management wants the market to believe the services hype, then Apple needs to prove to investors that services will continue growing rapidly despite potential challenges. If Apple is able to move its business away from cyclicality, and towards stable growth, then the stock will command a higher earnings multiple.
Outside of Apple's current services portfolio, Apple has its eye on key markets like autonomous driving, augmented reality, and original content programming. The first two are many years away from making a financial impact on Apple's business. The third business could take the form of a digital content streaming service. This business will have stiff competition from the likes of Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), and other traditional media companies like Disney (NYSE: DIS ) that are launching their own streaming services.
This is a highly competitive arena, with moats and competitive advantages difficult to establish. Often times, the quality of the content on the platform acts as a moat (brand) that economic investment can't outdo. Netflix's ability to create hit after hit has given it a solid reputation amongst its subscriber base. Because of this, much remains unknown about Apple's original content plans.
Apple Treats Its Shareholders Well, And Will Continue To Do So Apple is great about returning capital to shareholders, and has a pristine balance sheet. According to the now infamous Q4 letter, Apple has ~$130 billion in net cash (total cash less debt), a financial standing that makes most other companies envious. Apple continues to generate tens of billions in quarterly free cash flow, allowing this cash position to grow even further from here.
Right now, the company yields a dividend of $2.92, just under 2%, with a long-term share repurchase program of $100 billion. On top of general share price appreciation, stockholders are paid via quarterly dividend checks, and have a stock buyback working in their favor. These two reasons are the key reasons that Apple is a difficult stock to short. Buybacks provide a floor on share prices, while dividends act as costs to the short seller.
Apple also has an ability to make large-scale M&A moves. If Apple is serious about becoming a software company (as I believe it should be), utilizing its massive cash pile for something more productive than shareholder returns would be greatly rewarded by Wall Street. Think about it, if Apple spent billions of dollars on an acquisition of a software company, it would further the services growth story that the bulls believe in.
Valuation - An Updated Look At The DCF My Basic Estimates For Apple Current Prior Revenue (2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023) in billions $250.65, $260.75, $286.18, $292.62, $292.29 $277.61, $281.46, $301.38, $308.72, $315.36 EPS (2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023) on a per share basis $10.39, $10.97, $12.72, $13.01, $12.72 $12.58, $12.64, $13.70, $13.91, $14.05 Free Cash Flow (2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023) in billions $45.58, $48.2, $55.44, $56.95, $56.07 $54.2, $54.7, $59, $60.06, $60.81 Here are my calculations for CAPM:
This uses a 5.96% equity risk premium, an unlevered beta of 0.94, and a 10-year Treasury yield of 2.699%.
Here are my calculations for WACC:
This assumes a cost of debt of 3.1% derived from Apple's current bond yield, and a tax rate of 16.5%.
This leads me to a $187 target on Apple's shares, excluding capital returns like dividends.
A Warning On The Short-Term In the short-term, I believe Apple's volatility will continue and that the stock may have more room to fall. Catalysts like price cuts, emerging market weakness, and reports of production cuts could all weigh on the stock. In addition, if Apple releases a weak Q2 guidance when it reports, I would not be surprised for the stock to move down to retest lows off weak sentiment. My rating on Apple is based off the question: "What do you do if you don't own any Apple? Buy it here, sell it if you do own it, or hold onto it if you do own it?" Longer-term, I believe Apple's stock has upside. In the short-term it remains volatile.
Conclusion The iPhone faces many struggles over the next 12-18 months. Despite that, I believe a 5G iPhone will send profits and revenues surging, alleviating fear about the iPhone temporarily. Apple needs to shift away from hardware and towards software as quickly as possible if it is aiming for revenue stability. Utilization of its pristine balance sheet could allow the company to make massive M&A moves changing the Apple story away from iPhone. All in all, I expect some short-term volatility in shares, but the stock remains a great, long-term buy.
(Source: CNBC )
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, AMZN. it (other than from Seeking Alpha).
